title: The trade climate has already changed: Canberra is still adjusting too slowly
gist: Global trade-policy intervention in Jan-May 2026 ran at nearly double 2024 levels and ~25% above the 2025 average, the WTO's Yaoundé ministerial failed, and Australia - with 29% of exports going to China - is diversifying too slowly; the author urges plurilateral deals covering services, data and procurement, onshore mineral processing, and AI coalitions to avoid being a quarry for others' industrial strategies.

themes.theme: Record protectionism is the new operating system

insights.claim: A Trade Policy Activity Index from WTO and IMF sources shows global trade-policy intervention in January-May 2026 running at nearly double 2024 levels and about 25% above the 2025 average, the highest since tracking began after the GFC.
insights.speaker: Alicia García Herrero
insights.so_what: Structural rise in trade friction supports reshoring, tariff-hedged and domestic-champion trades.

insights.claim: The 2026 surge in trade intervention is driven by tariffs, import bans and subsidies, led by G20 governments with the rest of the world following, while trade-easing measures have lost momentum.
insights.speaker: Alicia García Herrero
insights.so_what: Expect continued subsidy-led industrial policy globally; margin risk for import-dependent sectors.
insights.locator: The surge is driven by tariffs

insights.claim: Industrial policy has been relegitimised and economic security has replaced commercial logic: the US has wrapped most imports in duties, Washington and Ottawa are not on speaking terms on trade, the EU proposes 'buy European' procurement, and China answers with export controls and state support.
insights.speaker: Alicia García Herrero
insights.so_what: US-Canada trade rupture and EU procurement preference are live sector risks; Chinese export controls threaten input supply.
insights.quote: Industrial policy has been relegitimised. Economic security has substituted any commercial logic.
insights.locator: This is the operating system Australia now trades in

insights.claim: Smaller economies copy protectionist scripts because the alternative is being the last open market in a closed neighbourhood.
insights.speaker: Alicia García Herrero
insights.so_what: Protectionism is contagious; expect diffusion to emerging markets.

insights.claim: First-quarter 2026 merchandise trade volumes still rose, lifted by semiconductor and AI-infrastructure demand, but this is not proof the old order holds: supply chains are being rewritten by statute.
insights.speaker: Alicia García Herrero
insights.so_what: Don't read resilient trade volumes as normalisation; AI hardware is masking deeper fragmentation.
insights.quote: Supply chains are being rewritten by statute.

insights.claim: The WTO's 14th Ministerial Conference in Yaoundé failed to agree even a modest reform package, did not restore dispute settlement, left the development/policy-space fight unresolved and let the e-commerce moratorium lapse.
insights.speaker: Alicia García Herrero
insights.so_what: Lapsed e-commerce moratorium opens the door to customs duties on digital transmissions — a risk for digital-services exporters.
insights.locator: There is no serious prospect that the WTO

insights.claim: The WTO deadlock is not temporary but reflects a world of large powers using trade as statecraft with no consensus left to constrain them; waiting for WTO reform is a strategy for arriving late.
insights.speaker: Alicia García Herrero
insights.so_what: Price in permanent absence of multilateral trade dispute resolution.
insights.quote: Waiting endlessly for WTO reform isn’t prudence. It is a strategy for arriving late.
insights.locator: Australia can stay open without staying sentimental

insights.claim: China took 29% of Australia's goods and services exports in 2025 and a quarter of two-way trade, with iron ore still dominating the relationship.
insights.speaker: Alicia García Herrero
insights.so_what: AUD, iron-ore miners and Australian terms of trade remain highly exposed to Chinese policy and steel demand.

insights.claim: The US is Australia's security guarantor, a growing export market, a source of critical technology and co-architect of AUKUS; both US and China relationships are now instruments of someone else's industrial strategy.
insights.speaker: Alicia García Herrero
insights.so_what: Australian assets carry dual great-power policy risk.

insights.claim: Australia risks exporting unprocessed rock into a market that no longer wants dependence on it while importing the finished green-tech and AI stack from Washington and Beijing.
insights.speaker: Alicia García Herrero
insights.so_what: Bearish long-run for a raw-commodity-only Australian model; bullish for domestic processing if policy follows.
insights.locator: The risk for countries that still preach openness

insights.claim: Canberra's steps so far — an EU free trade deal in March 2026, the UAE deal in force, a Singapore essential-supplies protocol, multi-billion-dollar US critical-minerals project lists, Trade 2040 and limited anti-dumping actions — are useful but lag the speed and scope of change elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Alicia García Herrero
insights.so_what: Australia-EU FTA and US critical-minerals pipelines are concrete tailwinds for exporters and miners.

insights.claim: Australia should not join the subsidy race or erect tariffs; being too small, specialised and trade-exposed, it should treat partnerships as infrastructure rather than communiqués.
insights.speaker: Alicia García Herrero
insights.so_what: Expect Australian policy to favour deal-making over subsidies — less fiscal support for domestic industry than US/EU.
insights.locator: Realism doesn’t mean joining the subsidy race

insights.claim: Australia should prioritise partners able to absorb more than bulk commodities — India, Southeast Asia, Japan, Korea, the EU and the Gulf — with agreements covering services, data and procurement; plurilateral deals among the willing will outperform consensus among 166 WTO members.
insights.speaker: Alicia García Herrero
insights.so_what: Watch for plurilateral/services-data agreements as catalysts for Australian services exporters.
insights.quote: Plurilateral deals among the willing will do more work than consensus among 166 members.

insights.claim: Australia should use its energy and mineral endowment to lock in processing and green-metals partnerships so it is not merely the quarry for other countries' net-zero plans.
insights.speaker: Alicia García Herrero
insights.so_what: Supports downstream-processing and green-metals project plays in Australia.
insights.quote: so the country isn’t merely the quarry for other countries’ net-zero plans
insights.locator: On investment, it means being equally serious

insights.claim: On AI, Australia should build energy, compute, skills and standards coalitions to reduce default dependence on America's AI hardware and models and increasingly on Chinese open-weight models.
insights.speaker: Alicia García Herrero
insights.so_what: Sovereign compute/data-centre and energy build-outs in Australia have policy support.
insights.locator: On investment, it means being equally serious

insights.claim: Australia should attract patient capital from like-minded partners while screening capital that arrives with political strings.
insights.speaker: Alicia García Herrero
insights.so_what: Tighter FDI screening likely for politically-linked capital, especially in resources.
insights.locator: On investment, it means being equally serious
